newsitem.title: USA: Clinton cancels three items with line-item veto.
newsitem.headline: Clinton cancels three items with line-item veto.

text.p: (New story)
By Arshad Mohammed

U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday struck down three items from the balanced-budget legislation he signed last week in the first use of the line-item veto, saving $600 million and drawing the ire of some Republicans.

Clinton's action was the first exercise of the line-item veto, a power sought by U.S. presidents for more than a century to cancel parts of spending bills and to strike down narrowly-targeted tax breaks.

The president took aim at two tax provisions: one that would have allowed financial services companies to shelter income in foreign tax havens and a second that would have given a tax break to certain food processing businesses.
He also struck down a provision that would have reduced the state of New York's spending on the Medicaid health care programme for the poor.

In making the announcement at the White House, Clinton described the veto as "a tool designed to fight against waste and unjustifiable expenditures, to insure government works for the public interest, not the private interests.

"From now on presidents will be able to say no to wasteful spending or tax loopholes even as they say yes to vital legislation," he added. "Special interests will not be able to play the old game of slipping a provision into a massive bill in the hope that no one will notice."
The veto has long been championed by Republicans, who included it in their "Contract with America" manifesto before they won control of both houses of Congress in 1994.

Congress passed the line-item veto last year, giving the power to Clinton, a Democrat, but stipulating he could not use it until January 1, 1997. Congress can ultimately overturn a veto with two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate.
A spokeswoman for Speaker of the House of Representatives Newt Gingrich, the main proponent of the "Contract with America," described Clinton's action as "petty politics."
"Disappointment and surprise are the usual side effects of having been blind-sided and today's line-item veto announcement is no exception," Gingrich spokeswoman Christina Martin said in a statement.
Martin said Gingrich and other Republican negotiators believed the White House had bargained in good faith in talks leading to Clinton's signing last week of balanced budget legislation.

"Now it appears that may not have been the case. No objections to these provisions were raised throughout the talks, therefore these vetoes may have less to do with sound politics and more to do with petty politics," she said.
White House officials denied the vetoes were political and said they informed Gingrich of their decision to use the veto.
They also offered the following details on the financial effect of the vetoes on the budget over the next five years:
-- cancelling the provision to allow U.S. financial services firms to avoid paying taxes on income from overseas operations would save the federal government $317 million;
-- vetoing the tax break to food processing companies that sell assets to certain farmers' cooperatives will save the government an estimated $98 milliion over five years;
-- and striking down preferential treatment for the state of New York regarding the Medicaid health care programme for the poor would save the federal government some $200 million.
The vetoes are expected to draw legal challenges, which Clinton said the White House expected to fend off.
Clinton said the 13 appropriations bills Congress is due to send him later in the year may also provide ripe targets for the veto.

"I'm hopeful that this will work out pretty much the way it did when I was (Arkansas state) governor -- that is when you know the president is prepared to use the line item veto that tends to operate as a deterrent against the most egregious kinds of project that would otherwise not be funded," Clinton said. "It would suit me if...the use of the veto became quite rare."
